source.title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
source.authors: Zheng-Fu He; Junxuan Wang; Rui Lin; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Qiong Tang; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures error patterns for Lorsa and SAEs and reports cross-method correlations, a different measurement relevant to whether sparse-decomposition errors have structure. It does not test the specific behaviors in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's dark-matter analysis compares Lorsa and SAE errors. It does not measure linear predictability from input activations, error scaling across SAE sizes, loss effects of replacing activations, two error components, or behavior lost by SAE-based analyses. Scaling-law results elsewhere compare reconstruction losses, not the listed dark-matter behaviors.
record.test_reason: The study is about Lorsa, a sparse replacement for attention layers. Its dark-matter appendix compares Lorsa errors with attention-output SAE errors on the same layers: layerwise FVU, per-token error norms, and per-token error cosine similarity. None of this measures what a version names. There is no linear prediction of SAE error from the input (V1), no comparison across SAE sizes (V2), no loss effect of splicing in reconstructions against random errors (V3), no split of the error into components (V4), no circuit or steering loss without the error term (V5), and no test of whether better training shrinks dark matter (V6). The cross-method error correlation is related to V2's 'fail on the same contexts' but compares different methods, not SAE sizes, so it goes under fits_no_version. The record's relation 'tests'/T2 contradicts its own finding that every version is not tested; it should be discusses/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors report a nontrivial correlation between Lorsa and attention-SAE errors in per-layer loss, per-token loss and error direction. They hypothesize 'universal dark matters' for sparse dictionary learning, arising from a shared gap with the model's representation structure or from difficulty capturing rare, nonlinear or dense components. They note that Lorsa's higher FVU and error norm may mean it captures more dark matter, because it predicts attention outputs rather than reconstructing its input. These are hypotheses; none is tested.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains Lorsa as a sparse replacement for attention modules and compares its errors with SAE errors; it does not reproduce the original SAE dark-matter analyses or their measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Error comparisons are shown across layers; the FVU comparison covers Pythia-160M and Llama-3.1-8B, while per-token error comparisons are shown for Pythia-160M.

fits_no_version.finding: Lorsa (trained to predict attention output from attention input) and attention-output SAEs on the same Pythia-160M layers show correlated errors: per-layer FVU, per-token error norms, and per-token error direction (cosine similarity over about 10,000 tokens). No numbers are stated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different sparse dictionary methods applied to the same layer leave correlated per-token errors, suggesting dark matter shared across methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Lorsa generally has higher FVU than the SAE, and both follow similar layerwise FVU trends in Pythia-160M and Llama-3.1-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layerwise reconstruction error profiles are similar across sparse decomposition methods.

record.problems: The dark-matter evidence is presented in figures without numerical values in the text. Per-token norms are plotted for only 64 tokens, and the reported cross-method correlation is not a comparison across SAE sizes. No uncertainty estimates or controls for these error analyses are stated.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from input activations.

Predictability of per-token error norms across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale. Appendix C's L(N,K) scaling-law figure for TopK SAEs reports convergence loss only, with no per-token error analysis and no stated values.
Loss effect of splicing in SAE reconstructions compared with random errors of equal norm.
Splitting the error into a linear part and a nonlinear part, and how each responds to further dictionary learning. The authors only speculate about 'nonlinear or dense components'.
Behaviour lost by SAE-based circuits or steering when the error term is dropped.
Whether dark matter is an artifact of SAE training. The authors hypothesize the opposite, a shared gap with the model's representation, but give no test.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Engels et al. (2410.14670) as the origin of the 'dark matter' framing. Its evidence is figure-only, with no uncertainty estimates, and the SAEs are attention-output SAEs. The record's relation and tranche are inconsistent with its own version statuses; the correct relation is discusses (T6).

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error vectors is a linear function of input activations.

Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale. The paper compares Lorsa and SAE errors, not multiple SAE sizes.
Whether replacing activations with SAE reconstructions harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linearly predictable error represents unlearned features and nonlinear error resists further dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-feature-based circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.
Whether dark matter is an SAE-training artifact or shrinks with alternative architectures or end-to-end training.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared the cosine similarity of Lorsa and SAE per-token error norms on the same contexts.
rows.measure: Distribution of cosine similarity between Lorsa and SAE per-token error norms
rows.note: The authors describe the error-pattern correlation as nontrivial and report positive correlation in per-token error-norm magnitudes and trends; no numerical cosine-similarity values are stated.
rows.check: Figure 14's caption calls the measure 'per-token error cosine similarity'. The Discussion lists 'error direction' as a correlated quantity, so this is most likely cosine similarity between Lorsa and SAE error vectors per token, not between error norms. The measure wording should be corrected. 'Observed' refers only to the authors' 'nontrivial correlation' remark; there are no numbers, and it bears on no version.
